slides.1: SDG 1 opens with an uncomfortable question. Can real poverty survive inside a developed society like Taiwan? It can, and it quietly decides how far a young person gets.
slides.2: SDG 1 asks governments to end poverty in every form. That includes low income, unsafe housing and weak social protection. The goal treats poverty as a fault in the system, not a personal failure.
slides.3: Taiwan has strong education, health care and technology, yet inequality has not disappeared. A household can look completely ordinary from outside while carrying debt, nursing a sick relative, or living on unstable work.
slides.4: Working poverty matters because effort alone no longer guarantees security. When parents are stuck with temporary contracts and low pay, they lose the hours and the energy their children need, so hardship travels into the next generation.
slides.5: Housing costs create poverty quietly. Once the rent takes too much of the income, every other need has to be cut, and students who move often or share a crowded room lose sleep, focus and confidence.
slides.6: Digital access has become part of basic opportunity. Without a reliable device, a stable connection and somebody to ask, students cannot fully join homework, research or AI learning, so their poverty is simply harder to see.
slides.7: Taiwan has built several safety nets, including health insurance, social welfare, emergency relief and local service centers. However, a good policy must also be easy to find, simple to apply for and respectful to use.
slides.8: Schools are powerful because they meet students every single day. Meal support, scholarships, counseling and after-school programs take real pressure off families, and a teacher who notices early becomes a bridge to community resources.
slides.9: Local organizations often understand a neighborhood better than any ministry does. They may provide food, tutoring, care or job information. Yet SDG 1 is not charity, because the goal is to give people choices, skills and dignity.
slides.10: Financial literacy hands students a practical kind of power. Learning about budgets, savings, debt, insurance and scams leads to better decisions, although education can never replace a fair wage.
slides.11: Data tools can reveal the poverty that nobody has counted. Students can map service locations, transport gaps or after-school resources, and a community then chooses more wisely. But every data point is still a real person.
slides.12: Service learning turns SDG 1 into something students have actually done. They can interview social workers, build bilingual resources or support tutoring, and their English improves because they are speaking for a real purpose.
slides.13: An aging society changes the shape of poverty. Older adults may live alone, manage illness, or struggle with services that have moved online, so SDG 1 now connects welfare, transport, health care and community.
slides.14: Poverty is harder to escape for migrant workers and new immigrant families, because language and paperwork build a wall around the help. If the process is confusing, many people simply stop asking for it.
slides.15: Climate risk is a poverty issue in disguise. When a disaster arrives, low-income families lose more and recover far more slowly, so shelters, insurance, clear information and community networks have to be ready first.
slides.16: Dignity changes the way support is given. Poverty should never be treated as shame or laziness, because many people are strong and simply face unfair conditions. Respectful help asks people what they actually need.
slides.17: In summary, SDG 1 is not only about money. It is about whether everyone can live with safety and with opportunity. Taiwan has clearly progressed, yet hidden poverty still asks us to improve access, timing and fairness.
slides.18: The most useful change may be our own language. Calling people lazy ends the conversation immediately, while asking which barriers they meet opens it, because we then have to discuss wages, rent, health, transport and education.
slides.19: Students are not too young to act on this. They can run bilingual campaigns, volunteer, collect stories, design simple tools, or present their findings to the school. PechaKucha turns private study into a public voice.
slides.20: Ending poverty sounds enormous, yet the action usually starts nearby. Notice a need, check the facts, speak respectfully and work with somebody else. If we connect English, the SDGs and action, students become real changemakers.
